newsitem.title: SINGAPORE: EU seeks WTO declaration on telecom pact.
newsitem.headline: EU seeks WTO declaration on telecom pact.

text.p: The European Union is pushing for a separate declaration on a global pact on freeing up basic telecommunications at the World Trade Organisation's ministerial conference, officials said on Tuesday.

They said the aim was to produce a text that could also be signed by the United States stating that a deal by the February 15 deadline in the sector, estimated to be worth well over $500 billion a year, was now in reach.

"The idea is to give a boost to the negotiations in Geneva," said one European official who asked not to be identified. But he said it was far from clear whether Washington -- which faces a strong telecoms lobby in Congress -- could go along.
"The EU wants to get the Americans on board, to commit themselves to reaching a deal now," he said.
The ministers from the 128-member WTO have already agreed to say in an overall declaration on opening world trade that they "intend to achieve a successful conclusion" in the Geneva talks.

The European official said the special statement, a text for which was still under discussion, would recognise that market opening offers expected in backstage talks at the conference had given encouragement for new optimism.
According to the official, the idea was raised at an experts' meeting on the fringes of the conference on Monday by Hong Kong and taken up enthusiastically by EU Trade Commissioner Sir Leon Brittan.

Singapore, one of the key markets the United States wants to see opened up, has already signalled it has a new offer in the works, and other major emerging economies are expected to make fresh proposals this week.
But Brazil, one of the major developing countries in the sector, is understood to be resisting pressure to come up with a plan to move faster towards liberalisation.

An earlier effort to negotiate a WTO pact collapsed in April when the United States, which argues it has the most open telecoms market in the world, said there was not a sufficient "critical mass" of offers for it to sign up.

U.S. industry has insisted that if it is to open up its own market to all-comers under the WTO's basic principle of most-favoured-nation (MFN) treatment for trade partners, it has to have at least similar -- if not fully equal -- access to other markets.
A total of 48 countries, counting all l5 EU members separately, have made offers since talks on a pact began in 1995. Last month both Brussels and Washington tabled improved offers of their own.
